notes.note: مَرْمَر is given as 'alabaster' in contrast to رُخَام 'marble'. In general MSA مَرْمَر also means marble; the alabaster sense is the local Egyptian usage behind 'مسجد المرمر'. Correct for the story, but a learner may later meet مَرْمَر = marble; a short gloss '(here: alabaster)' would help.
دَلِيلَتُكُمُ (your guide, f.) is understandable but unusual; دَلِيل is normally used for both genders (أَنَا دَلِيلُكُمُ الْيَوْمَ) or مُرْشِدَتُكُمْ for a female guide. Style only.

مُرْفَق مَعَ هٰذِهِ الرِّسَالَة سِيرَتِي الذَّاتِيَّة is marked wrong and مُرْفَقَة right. With the predicate fronted before a compound subject (CV + certificate), agreement with the nearest noun is the usual rule, so مُرْفَقَة is fine, but invariable مُرْفَق ('Attached: …') is also extremely common in real letters. Consider softening 'wrong' to 'less careful'.

notes.note: Day 82 vocalises the formula without tanwīn (تَحِيَّة طَيِّبَة, pausal) and day 84 with the accusative tanwīn (تَحِيَّةً طَيِّبَةً), which is the fully-vocalised form. Both are accepted, but the two days should agree, since the learner is told the frame is 'fixed'.

الْمُشْكِلَةَ الْأَكْبَرَ: with the definite article the elative traditionally agrees in gender (الْمُشْكِلَةُ الْكُبْرَى). 'المشكلة الأكبر' is very common in modern press Arabic, so not reported as an error, but الْكُبْرَى would be the safer model for a course that teaches case and agreement.
tap gloss 'أَهَمُّ=the most important' appears in a comparative sentence (أَهَمُّ مِنَ …, 'more important than'); the segs are right, only the shared tap gloss shows the superlative sense.
«يَعْنِي» وَ«كَيْفَ أَقُولُ» تُعْطِيكَ وَقْتًا: two quoted phrases as subject would strictly take the dual تُعْطِيَانِكَ; treating them as a non-human plural with f. sg. is tolerated. Style only.
Story logic: 'It's the second-to-last week of the course' but day 88 is in week 13, the last week (day 85 says 'the first day of the last week').

The hamza-seat rule (kasra → yāʾ, ḍamma → wāw, otherwise alif) is a deliberate simplification; it does not cover long vowels, initial hamza or final hamza after sukūn (شَيْء, written on the line). Fine for the course level, but the learner may apply it to words like شَيْء; a one-line caveat could help.
In the list of the six non-joining letters, the tap on و says 'و=and'; in this context it is the letter wāw (the other five taps correctly give letter names).
Engine capitalisation of names is inconsistent: 'masjidu muḥammad ʿAlī' (lower-case Muḥammad, capital ʿAlī), 'ṣalāḥi d-dīn' lower-case. Cosmetic.
The shared tap gloss 'لَا=no' appears inside لَا أُوَافِقُ (I do NOT agree), where 'not' is meant; segs in the dialogues say 'not'. Minor tap-gloss sense mismatch.

summary: I read all 3,123 lines of audit/days-81-90.txt (days 81-90: passive, formal letter, debate connectors, Week 12 review, listening/reading/speaking/writing reviews, final exam, next steps) and checked every Arabic string, its harakat and case endings, agreement, verb forms, translations and literals, seg and tap glosses, quiz answer keys and the transliteration against the Arabic. The Arabic itself is clean: I found no misspelt word, wrong case ending, wrong agreement, wrong mood or wrong answer key in the sentences, dialogues, readings or quizzes. The 16 reported errors are 3 major gloss errors (اِكْتَشَفَ glossed as passive 'was discovered'; قِيلَ glossed 'it is said' on a distractor whose prompt is 'it is said'; عَبَّرَ glossed as an imperative and the neighbouring past verbs glossed in the present), 5 minor gloss/answer-key issues (shared tap glosses pulled from other sentences: 'ten (part of fifteen)', 'at the hour', 'the address', 'you're welcome'; a tap on the wrong form claiming '-a after an'; a grammatical iḍāfa marked 'wrong'), and 7 engine findings, of which 3 are major because they produce non-words the learner will read aloud: the hamzat-waṣl maṣdars after al- (الِاسْتِمَاع/الِامْتِحَان/الِاحْتِرَام → 'liāstimāʿ', 'Iliāmtiḥān', 'liāḥtirām' in titles and formulas of days 82, 84, 85, 87, 89), standalone الَّذِي/الَّتِي → 'Illadhī/Illatī', and وَبِالْإِضَافَةِ → 'Wabiālʾiḍāfati'; the minor ones are the known bare-letter and وَ-name quirks, final -āy/-āw rendered as vowels, and 'ashalu' for أَسْهَلُ. Pattern: the content author's segs are consistently right while the shared tap vocabulary occasionally carries a sense from another day; and the transliteration engine mishandles every word whose hamzat waṣl is written with a kasra under the alif of al-.
